newsitem.title: USA: FEATURE - US investors question EMU optimism.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - US investors question EMU optimism.

text.p: Standing outside all the hype, U.S. investors are taking a sceptical line on Europe's plans for a single currency.
Although most have joined the yield convergence trades for European economic and monetary union (EMU) which have been the most profitable transactions of 1999, misgivings remain.

The U.S. worries are similar to those of European investors who believe that financial markets have priced in too much economic progress by peripheral EU countries, and that the social costs of the process will ultimately prove too high.
But distance seems to magnify these anxieties.

"We could actually see them begin this process and (see it lead to) a big social blowup, but that's far beyond the horizons we usually look at. We have to go with the flow," said Craig Larimer, head of international market analysis at First Chicago Capital Markets.

A single European currency, the main feature of EMU, is due to for launch on January 1, 1999. To qualify, various members of the 15-nation European Union have subjected themselves to a severe fiscal clampdown.
U.S. analysts say many European countries seem to be including dubious projections on revenue in order to make the numbers add up.
But just as fast as official forecasts have shifted, so has the market's view on which countries will make it.

After currency turmoil in 1992 and 1993, many thought EMU's chances of success were slim. Then, they reckoned a few "core" European countries would qualify. Nowadays, a growing number are talking about peripheral countries getting in.
"The markets are manic-depressive about EMU," said Lee Thomas, senior international portfolio manager at Pacific Investment Management Co. (PIMCO).
"First we thought EMU was not going to make it. Then we believed it would make it with a small group. Now, we've got Spain and Italy in the first round, which is extremely unlikely," Thomas said.

PIMCO is banking on Ireland and Finland as unlikely first-team EMU members, though the most likely inaugural crowd includes Germany, France, the Netherlands, Austria, Belgium and Luxembourg, Thomas said.
"Those are low-risk convergence trades. There would have to be some kind of political negotiation to get Italy and Spain in," he added.
But along with the optimism over EMU have come some large moves in the market, many of which have been too tempting for investors in the U.S. to pass up.

The Italian lira, for instance, has rallied to less than 1,000 per mark in recent weeks, as hopes mount that Italy will meet stiff convergence EMU criteria. That is some 10 percent stronger than at the start of the year and compares with a record lowpoint of 1275 per mark in March 1995.

The lira has powered ahead despite a few roadblocks by prominent European authorities. Politicians and central bankers from French President Jacques Chirac to Bundesbank council members have recently downplayed the likelihood or the wisdom of Italy joining an initial single currency bloc.
"I just think there's too much euphoria about some of these countries qualifying," said Earl Johnson, foreign exhange economist at the Bank of Montreal.
EMU trades in the currency market have been mirrored by the convergence of high-yield government bonds, as confidence grows that the economies of member states will converge successfully.

Swedish 10-year paper, yielding about 125 basis points over comparable Bunds, has narrowed sharply from nearly 300 a year ago. The Spanish benchmark spread is 180 basis points over Bunds, compared with 448 last October. Finnish 10-year spreads are around 50 basis points over Bunds, versus 200 18 months ago.
PIMCO's Thomas said he has gone along with the convergence play on the Spanish peseta, the Swedish crown and the lira, but has reduced those positions recently.
As in Europe, investors in the U.S. can only guess at the possible valuation for each currency as it enters EMU. Along with that they have to weigh the impact on the dollar.

With aggregate European Union GDP rivalling U.S. GDP, a complete conversion of European currencies to the proposed euro single unit could prompt calls to supplant the dollar as the world's reserve currency, analysts maintain.
But for all the ramifications EMU has for U.S. companies doing business in Europe, analysts note very few have taken steps to minimise their potential foreign exchange risks.
"We should start to see some preparation from corporates, but I don't get the feeling a lot of them are running around deciding what to do in terms of hedging," Johnson said.
